Definite Integration — JEE Main revision guide

A definite integral adds many tiny contributions. A graph turns those contributions into signed strips of area. Symmetry can pair the strips before we do any long integration.

Source difficulties before studying

Official Unit 8 includes the fundamental theorem, properties and evaluation of definite integrals. The supplied source also includes elementary improper-integral examples with logarithmic endpoints or an infinite upper limit. We teach the needed endpoint limits, without assuming an advanced Beta/Gamma course.

Q12 has an answer-key error as printed. The two-sided limit does not exist. Its right-hand limit is 2/32/32/3, but its left-hand limit is −2/3-2/3−2/3. The keyed 0.670.670.67 applies only if the intended question was x→0+x\to0^+x→0+. We preserve the original two-sided question and explain the difference.

Read Q3's options carefully: π/4\pi/4π/4 and π2/4\pi^2/4π2/4 are different. Q18 and Q32 require splitting at changes of formula. For Q31, do not replace π\piπ by 22/722/722/7; the small difference is the exact answer.

Concept C01 — From tiny rectangles to one signed total

Divide [a,b][a,b][a,b] into nnn equal widths Δx=(b−a)/n\Delta x=(b-a)/nΔx=(b−a)/n. A narrow strip at input xrx_rxr​ has approximate signed area f(xr)Δxf(x_r)\Delta xf(xr​)Δx. Adding them and shrinking the widths gives

∫abf(x) dx=lim⁡n→∞∑r=1nf(xr)Δx\boxed{\int_a^b f(x)\,dx =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=1}^n f(x_r)\Delta x}∫ab​f(x)dx=n→∞lim​r=1∑n​f(xr​)Δx​

for a continuous function. Some functions with jumps, such as the floor function, also work: their strip sums still approach one total. When that total exists in this sense, we call the function Riemann-integrable. aaa is the lower limit, bbb the upper limit. The result is a number when both limits are fixed.

For a<ba<ba<b, strips above the axis contribute positively and strips below it negatively:

signed integral=area above−area below.\text{signed integral}=\text{area above}-\text{area below}.signed integral=area above−area below.

Total geometric area uses ∫ab∣f(x)∣dx\int_a^b|f(x)|dx∫ab​∣f(x)∣dx. For f(x)=xf(x)=xf(x)=x on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], the signed total is 000 but the total area is 111.

Fundamental theorem — Important for JEE Main. If F′=fF'=fF′=f and fff is continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b],

∫abf(x) dx=F(b)−F(a).\boxed{\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)}.∫ab​f(x)dx=F(b)−F(a)​.

The notation [F(x)]ab[F(x)]_a^b[F(x)]ab​ means this upper value minus lower value. The constant cancels, so do not add +C+C+C to the final definite number. The letter inside is a dummy variable: ∫abf(x)dx=∫abf(t)dt\int_a^b f(x)dx=\int_a^b f(t)dt∫ab​f(x)dx=∫ab​f(t)dt.

Concept C02 — Basic properties and size checks

For integrable functions and limits where the expressions are defined:

∫aaf=0,∫abf=−∫baf,∫acf=∫abf+∫bcf,∫ab(αf+βg)=α∫abf+β∫abg.\begin{gathered} \int_a^a f=0,\qquad \int_a^b f=-\int_b^a f,\qquad \int_a^c f=\int_a^b f+\int_b^c f,\\ \int_a^b(\alpha f+\beta g)=\alpha\int_a^b f+\beta\int_a^b g. \end{gathered}∫aa​f=0,∫ab​f=−∫ba​f,∫ac​f=∫ab​f+∫bc​f,∫ab​(αf+βg)=α∫ab​f+β∫ab​g.​

Here α,β\alpha,\betaα,β are constants. For a<ba<ba<b:

f≥0⇒∫abf≥0,f≤g⇒∫abf≤∫abg.f\ge0\Rightarrow\int_a^b f\ge0,\qquad f\le g\Rightarrow\int_a^b f\le\int_a^b g.f≥0⇒∫ab​f≥0,f≤g⇒∫ab​f≤∫ab​g.

If m≤f(x)≤Mm\le f(x)\le Mm≤f(x)≤M throughout [a,b][a,b][a,b],

m(b−a)≤∫abf≤M(b−a).m(b-a)\le\int_a^b f\le M(b-a).m(b−a)≤∫ab​f≤M(b−a).

Meaning: the true strip heights lie between two rectangle heights. The average value of fff is

favg=1b−a∫abf(x) dx.f_{\rm avg}=\frac1{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.favg​=b−a1​∫ab​f(x)dx.

For continuous fff, this average is attained at some input in [a,b][a,b][a,b].

Important for JEE Main — bounds and sign checks:

∣∫abf∣≤∫ab∣f∣,(∫abf)2≤(b−a)∫abf2.\left|\int_a^b f\right|\le\int_a^b|f|,\qquad \left(\int_a^b f\right)^2\le(b-a)\int_a^b f^2.​∫ab​f​≤∫ab​∣f∣,(∫ab​f)2≤(b−a)∫ab​f2.

The second is the integral Cauchy–Schwarz bound; it requires a finite integral of f2f^2f2 and a<ba<ba<b. For continuous fff, it also follows from ∫ab(f−favg)2≥0\int_a^b(f-f_{\rm avg})^2\ge0∫ab​(f−favg​)2≥0; expanding leaves the displayed inequality. Equality then needs fff constant. This is useful for estimating an integral when its exact primitive is awkward.

Concept C03 — Substitution and parts still work, with limits

Important for JEE Main. When u=g(x)u=g(x)u=g(x) is a suitable differentiable monotone substitution on the interval, change the bounds together with the integrand:

∫abf(g(x))g′(x)dx=∫g(a)g(b)f(u) du.\int_a^b f(g(x))g'(x)dx =\int_{g(a)}^{g(b)}f(u)\,du.∫ab​f(g(x))g′(x)dx=∫g(a)g(b)​f(u)du.

A decreasing substitution reverses the order of the new bounds; its negative differential handles that reversal. Never use uuu inside and the old xxx bounds outside. If a change of variable is not monotone, split into suitable pieces where necessary. A valid chain-rule primitive can still be used without a one-to-one change of coordinates.

For parts:

∫abu v′ dx=[uv]ab−∫abu′v dx.\boxed{\int_a^b u\,v'\,dx=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b u'v\,dx}.∫ab​uv′dx=[uv]ab​−∫ab​u′vdx​.

Pick uuu whose derivative simplifies. Example: u=tan⁡−1xu=\tan^{-1}xu=tan−1x, dv=x dxdv=x\,dxdv=xdx turns inverse tangent into 1/(1+x2)1/(1+x^2)1/(1+x2).

Carry forward the important indefinite tools:

∫dx1+x2=tan⁡−1x+C,∫g′gdx=ln⁡∣g∣+C,∫xndx=xn+1n+1+C (n≠−1).\int\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\tan^{-1}x+C,\quad \int\frac{g'}g dx=\ln|g|+C,\quad \int x^n dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\ (n\ne-1).∫1+x2dx​=tan−1x+C,∫gg′​dx=ln∣g∣+C,∫xndx=n+1xn+1​+C (n=−1).

Simplify first: polynomial division, a conjugate, product-to-sum, or a derivative match can avoid a long primitive.

Concept C04 — Reflection pairs equal distances from the midpoint

Important for JEE Main. On [a,b][a,b][a,b], put u=a+b−xu=a+b-xu=a+b−x. An input near the left end pairs with one equally far from the right end:

∫abf(x) dx=∫abf(a+b−x) dx.\boxed{\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\int_a^b f(a+b-x)\,dx}.∫ab​f(x)dx=∫ab​f(a+b−x)dx​.

Why? As xxx runs left to right, uuu runs right to left; dx=−dudx=-dudx=−du restores the order. The interval and strip widths stay the same.

Let the integral be III. Write its reflected version and add:

2I=∫ab[f(x)+f(a+b−x)]dx.2I=\int_a^b[f(x)+f(a+b-x)]dx.2I=∫ab​[f(x)+f(a+b−x)]dx.

If the pair sum is the constant KKK, then

I=K(b−a)2.\boxed{I=\frac{K(b-a)}2}.I=2K(b−a)​​.

For sin⁡px/(sin⁡px+cos⁡px)\sin^p x/(\sin^p x+\cos^p x)sinpx/(sinpx+cospx) on [0,π/2][0,\pi/2][0,π/2], p>0p>0p>0, reflection swaps sine and cosine. The pair sum is 111, so the answer is π/4\pi/4π/4. This is often shorter than finding any primitive.

Log clue: if h(x)h(a+b−x)=K>0h(x)h(a+b-x)=K>0h(x)h(a+b−x)=K>0 and both log integrals exist, then the logs add to ln⁡K\ln KlnK. Integrate the sum rather than each difficult log separately.

Concept C05 — Symmetric weight: replace x by the midpoint

Suppose h(a+b−x)=h(x)h(a+b-x)=h(x)h(a+b−x)=h(x) and both relevant integrals exist. Set I=∫abxh(x)dxI=\int_a^b xh(x)dxI=∫ab​xh(x)dx and reflect:

I=∫ab(a+b−x)h(x)dx.I=\int_a^b(a+b-x)h(x)dx.I=∫ab​(a+b−x)h(x)dx.

Add the two:

∫abxh(x)dx=a+b2∫abh(x)dx.\boxed{\int_a^b xh(x)dx=\frac{a+b}2\int_a^b h(x)dx}.∫ab​xh(x)dx=2a+b​∫ab​h(x)dx​.

Meaning: the equal weights at two paired inputs have average input (a+b)/2(a+b)/2(a+b)/2.

Do not replace xxx by the midpoint in an arbitrary integrand. The symmetry of the remaining factor is the condition. On [0,π][0,\pi][0,π], both sin⁡x/(1+cos⁡2x)\sin x/(1+\cos^2x)sinx/(1+cos2x) and 1/(1+sin⁡x)1/(1+\sin x)1/(1+sinx) have this symmetry.

Concept C06 — Even, odd and complementary exponential weights

Important for JEE Main. On a symmetric interval [−a,a][-a,a][−a,a], assuming integrability:

f(−x)=f(x)⇒∫−aaf=2∫0af(even),f(−x)=−f(x)⇒∫−aaf=0(odd).\begin{aligned} f(-x)=f(x)&\Rightarrow\int_{-a}^a f=2\int_0^a f &&\text{(even)},\\ f(-x)=-f(x)&\Rightarrow\int_{-a}^a f=0 &&\text{(odd)}. \end{aligned}f(−x)=f(x)f(−x)=−f(x)​⇒∫−aa​f=2∫0a​f⇒∫−aa​f=0​​(even),(odd).​

An even graph mirrors in the vertical axis. An odd graph matches after a half-turn about the origin; opposite signed strips cancel. x2sin⁡xx^2\sin xx2sinx is odd because even times odd is odd. x∣x∣x|x|x∣x∣ is also odd. Do not treat a positive even function such as cos⁡x\cos xcosx on [−π/2,π/2][-\pi/2,\pi/2][−π/2,π/2] as a cancelling one.

For an odd function ggg, the complementary pair

11+eg(x)+11+e−g(x)=1\frac1{1+e^{g(x)}}+\frac1{1+e^{-g(x)}}=11+eg(x)1​+1+e−g(x)1​=1

can simplify a non-even integrand. If www is even,

∫−aaw(x)1+eg(x)dx=12∫−aaw(x)dx.\boxed{\int_{-a}^a\frac{w(x)}{1+e^{g(x)}}dx =\frac12\int_{-a}^a w(x)dx}.∫−aa​1+eg(x)w(x)​dx=21​∫−aa​w(x)dx​.

The whole integrand is usually not even; pairing proves the result. This handles Q2 with g=x,w=sin⁡2xg=x,w=\sin^2xg=x,w=sin2x and Q20 with g=sin⁡x,w=1g=\sin x,w=1g=sinx,w=1.

Concept C07 — Periods, modulus waves and complete cycles

If f(x+T)=f(x)f(x+T)=f(x)f(x+T)=f(x), T>0T>0T>0, and fff is integrable over a period:

∫cc+Tf(x)dx=∫0Tf(x)dx,∫0nTf=n∫0Tf\int_c^{c+T}f(x)dx=\int_0^Tf(x)dx,\qquad \int_0^{nT}f=n\int_0^Tf∫cc+T​f(x)dx=∫0T​f(x)dx,∫0nT​f=n∫0T​f

for a positive integer nnn. For a noninteger number of periods, separate the full periods and the remaining part.

Important for JEE Main: ∣sin⁡x∣|\sin x|∣sinx∣ has period π\piπ, with one-period integral 222. Ordinary sin⁡x\sin xsinx has period 2π2\pi2π, with one-period signed integral 000.

Do not use “twice the first half” unless the second half really has the same signed contribution. For sin⁡3x\sin^3xsin3x, the second π\piπ-interval contributes the negative of the first.

For R=A2+B2>0R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}>0R=A2+B2​>0, Asin⁡x+Bcos⁡x=Rsin⁡(x+ϕ)A\sin x+B\cos x=R\sin(x+\phi)Asinx+Bcosx=Rsin(x+ϕ). Thus its absolute value has period π\piπ and one-period integral 2R2R2R. A phase shift does not change an integral over a whole period.

Product-to-sum is useful when frequencies differ:

2sin⁡Acos⁡B=sin⁡(A+B)+sin⁡(A−B).2\sin A\cos B=\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B).2sinAcosB=sin(A+B)+sin(A−B).

For integer k≠0k\ne0k=0, ∫0πsin⁡(kx)dx=[1−(−1)k]/k\int_0^\pi\sin(kx)dx=[1-(-1)^k]/k∫0π​sin(kx)dx=[1−(−1)k]/k. An odd harmonic gives 2/k2/k2/k, an even one 000.

Concept C08 — Modulus and floor: find all change points first

Important for JEE Main. Before removing ∣g(x)∣|g(x)|∣g(x)∣, solve g(x)=0g(x)=0g(x)=0 and test the sign between roots.

∣g∣={g,g≥0,−g,g<0.|g|=\begin{cases}g,&g\ge0,\\-g,&g<0.\end{cases}∣g∣={g,−g,​g≥0,g<0.​

For ∣x2−x∣|x^2-x|∣x2−x∣, the inside is negative on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) and positive on (1,2)(1,2)(1,2). The negative piece is reflected above the axis.

The floor [u]=⌊u⌋[u]=\lfloor u\rfloor[u]=⌊u⌋ is the greatest integer not exceeding uuu. For [x2][x^2][x2], changes occur where x2x^2x2 crosses an integer:

[x2]={0,0≤x<1,1,1≤x<2,2,2≤x<3,3,3≤x<2.[x^2]= \begin{cases} 0,&0\le x<1,\\ 1,&1\le x<\sqrt2,\\ 2,&\sqrt2\le x<\sqrt3,\\ 3,&\sqrt3\le x<2. \end{cases}[x2]=⎩⎨⎧​0,1,2,3,​0≤x<1,1≤x<2​,2​≤x<3​,3​≤x<2.​

Height times width gives each rectangular area. The single endpoint value [22]=4[2^2]=4[22]=4 contributes no width, hence no area. More generally, changing finitely many point values does not change a bounded Riemann integral.

Important for JEE Main. For Sn=∫0π/2sin⁡nx dxS_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x\,dxSn​=∫0π/2​sinnxdx, nonnegative integer nnn,

S2m=1⋅3⋯(2m−1)2⋅4⋯2mπ2,S2m+1=2⋅4⋯2m3⋅5⋯(2m+1).S_{2m}=\frac{1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)}{2\cdot4\cdots2m}\frac\pi2,\quad S_{2m+1}=\frac{2\cdot4\cdots2m}{3\cdot5\cdots(2m+1)}.S2m​=2⋅4⋯2m1⋅3⋯(2m−1)​2π​,S2m+1​=3⋅5⋯(2m+1)2⋅4⋯2m​.

Use S0,S1S_0,S_1S0​,S1​ directly for the base cases. For ∫0πsin⁡nx dx\int_0^\pi\sin^n x\,dx∫0π​sinnxdx, reflection gives 2Sn2S_n2Sn​.

If one power in sin⁡mxcos⁡nx\sin^m x\cos^n xsinmxcosnx is odd, saving one derivative factor and substituting is often shorter than a recurrence. Q30 uses u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx.

For nonnegative integers m,nm,nm,n, a useful finite-parts result is

∫01xm(1−x)ndx=m! n!(m+n+1)!.\int_0^1x^m(1-x)^n dx=\frac{m!\,n!}{(m+n+1)!}.∫01​xm(1−x)ndx=(m+n+1)!m!n!​.

It follows by parts: Jm,n=nm+1Jm+1,n−1J_{m,n}=\frac n{m+1}J_{m+1,n-1}Jm,n​=m+1n​Jm+1,n−1​ for n≥1n\ge1n≥1, ending with Jm+n,0=1/(m+n+1)J_{m+n,0}=1/(m+n+1)Jm+n,0​=1/(m+n+1). Concept C10 — The derivative of accumulated area

For continuous fff, define A(x)=∫axf(t)dtA(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dtA(x)=∫ax​f(t)dt. Increasing xxx by a tiny hhh adds a strip with approximate area f(x)hf(x)hf(x)h. Therefore

A′(x)=f(x).\boxed{A'(x)=f(x)}.A′(x)=f(x)​.

With a changing upper input v(x)v(x)v(x), chain rule adds its rate:

ddx∫av(x)f(t)dt=f(v(x))v′(x).\frac d{dx}\int_a^{v(x)}f(t)dt=f(v(x))v'(x).dxd​∫av(x)​f(t)dt=f(v(x))v′(x).

If both ends move:

ddx∫u(x)v(x)f(t)dt=f(v(x))v′(x)−f(u(x))u′(x).\boxed{\frac d{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)dt =f(v(x))v'(x)-f(u(x))u'(x)}.dxd​∫u(x)v(x)​f(t)dt=f(v(x))v′(x)−f(u(x))u′(x)​.

Upper end adds; lower end removes. This is a signed formula, so it still works when the upper value is less than the lower value, provided the function is regular on the needed interval.

The rule above assumes the integrand depends on the dummy variable ttt, not additionally on the external xxx. An integral with xxx also inside the integrand needs that dependence handled; do not apply this rule mechanically.

Look at the limits before differentiating.

  • ∫01tf(t)dt\int_0^1tf(t)dt∫01​tf(t)dt is a fixed number. Rename it CCC and solve the resulting ordinary equation.
  • ∫0xf(t)dt\int_0^x f(t)dt∫0x​f(t)dt changes with xxx. Its derivative is f(x)f(x)f(x).

For Q21,

f(x)=x+C,C=∫01t(t+C)dt=13+C2.f(x)=x+C,\qquad C=\int_0^1t(t+C)dt=\frac13+\frac C2.f(x)=x+C,C=∫01​t(t+C)dt=31​+2C​.

The unknown function has become one unknown number.

For F(x)=∫0x(t2−3t+2)dtF(x)=\int_0^x(t^2-3t+2)dtF(x)=∫0x​(t2−3t+2)dt, the derivative is (x−1)(x−2)(x-1)(x-2)(x−1)(x−2). Its sign tells where the accumulated signed area grows or shrinks. This is the link to Applications of Derivatives.

Concept C12 — Rectangle sums and products with many factors

Important for JEE Main. The standard pattern is

1n∑r=1nf(rn)⟶∫01f(t)dt\boxed{\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^n f\left(\frac rn\right) \longrightarrow\int_0^1f(t)dt}n1​r=1∑n​f(nr​)⟶∫01​f(t)dt​

for continuous fff. Here 1/n1/n1/n is the strip width and r/nr/nr/n its right-end sample input.

Do the scaling explicitly:

rn2+r2=1nr/n1+(r/n)2.\frac r{n^2+r^2} =\frac1n\frac{r/n}{1+(r/n)^2}.n2+r2r​=n1​1+(r/n)2r/n​.

Now the strip-height function is f(t)=t/(1+t2)f(t)=t/(1+t^2)f(t)=t/(1+t2).

For [a,b][a,b][a,b], use Δx=(b−a)/n\Delta x=(b-a)/nΔx=(b−a)/n, sample input a+rΔxa+r\Delta xa+rΔx, and the matching factor Δx\Delta xΔx. A sum without the right width may tend to infinity or need an extra scaling factor.

A product becomes a sum after taking logs. For positive continuous hhh on [0,1][0,1][0,1],

[∏r=1nh(r/n)]1/n⟶exp⁡(∫01ln⁡h(t)dt).\left[\prod_{r=1}^n h(r/n)\right]^{1/n} \longrightarrow \exp\left(\int_0^1\ln h(t)dt\right).[r=1∏n​h(r/n)]1/n⟶exp(∫01​lnh(t)dt).

First remove any growing powers of nnn. In Q14, each factor n+r=n(1+r/n)n+r=n(1+r/n)n+r=n(1+r/n), and there are exactly nnn factors. The external 1/n1/n1/n cancels their nnnth-root factor nnn. Only then take logs.

Concept C13 — An endpoint infinity needs a limit

Supporting source examples. An improper integral has an infinite bound or an integrand that becomes unbounded at a bound or inside the interval.

∫0∞f=lim⁡R→∞∫0Rf,∫0bf=lim⁡ε→0+∫εbf\int_0^\infty f=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^Rf,\qquad \int_0^b f=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\int_\varepsilon^b f∫0∞​f=R→∞lim​∫0R​f,∫0b​f=ε→0+lim​∫εb​f

when the indicated limits exist finitely. An interior singularity needs separate limits on its two sides. Opposite infinities cannot be cancelled and called an ordinary improper integral.

Useful convergence clues:

∫01x−pdx converges iff p<1,∫1∞x−pdx converges iff p>1.\int_0^1x^{-p}dx\text{ converges iff }p<1,\qquad \int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx\text{ converges iff }p>1.∫01​x−pdx converges iff p<1,∫1∞​x−pdx converges iff p>1.

Also ∫01∣ln⁡x∣dx=1\int_0^1|\ln x|dx=1∫01​∣lnx∣dx=1. An unbounded height may still give a finite area because the strip widths near the endpoint become very small.

Near zero, sin⁡x/x→1\sin x/x\to1sinx/x→1, so ln⁡(sin⁡x)=ln⁡x+ln⁡(sin⁡x/x)\ln(\sin x)=\ln x+\ln(\sin x/x)ln(sinx)=lnx+ln(sinx/x). The second term stays bounded, while ln⁡x\ln xlnx has a convergent integral. This justifies the log-sine endpoint in Q5.

For c>0c>0c>0 and a nonnegative integer nnn,

∫0∞xne−cxdx=n!cn+1.\int_0^\infty x^ne^{-cx}dx=\frac{n!}{c^{n+1}}.∫0∞​xne−cxdx=cn+1n!​.

Derive it by parts nnn times, starting with ∫0∞e−cxdx=1/c\int_0^\infty e^{-cx}dx=1/c∫0∞​e−cxdx=1/c. Every polynomial-times-exponential boundary term tends to zero at infinity. This elementary result handles Q22; it is not permission to ignore convergence.

Concept C14 — Limits with a short integral: look at the interval size

If fff is continuous at aaa,

1h∫aa+hf(t)dt→f(a)\boxed{\frac1h\int_a^{a+h}f(t)dt\to f(a)}h1​∫aa+h​f(t)dt→f(a)​

as h→0h\to0h→0 through allowed inputs. It is the average height over a short interval.

If f(t)f(t)f(t) behaves like ctpct^pctp as t→0+t\to0^+t→0+, p>−1p>-1p>−1, then for u→0+u\to0^+u→0+,

∫0uf(t)dt∼cp+1up+1.\int_0^u f(t)dt\sim\frac c{p+1}u^{p+1}.∫0u​f(t)dt∼p+1c​up+1.

The symbol ∼\sim∼ means the ratio tends to 111 when the leading comparison is nonzero. The statement follows by bounding f(t)f(t)f(t) between (c−ε)tp(c-\varepsilon)t^p(c−ε)tp and (c+ε)tp(c+\varepsilon)t^p(c+ε)tp for small positive ttt; it is not a rule for ignoring signs.

Important sign check in Q12: sin⁡t∼t\sin\sqrt t\sim\sqrt tsint​∼t​, so

∫0x2sin⁡t dt∼23(x2)3/2=23∣x∣3.\int_0^{x^2}\sin\sqrt t\,dt \sim\frac23(x^2)^{3/2} =\frac23|x|^3.∫0x2​sint​dt∼32​(x2)3/2=32​∣x∣3.

Dividing by x3x^3x3 leaves different signs on the two sides. Always use x2=∣x∣\sqrt{x^2}=|x|x2​=∣x∣.

An expansion or L'Hôpital check can be useful, but the domain/sign analysis must come first. For the printed two-sided question, finding only the right-side value is incomplete.

Concept C15 — Choose the route before doing long algebra

Visible clue Short route and its reason
Sine/cosine swapped by x↦π/2−xx\mapsto\pi/2-xx↦π/2−x Pair reflected integrands; their sum may be 111
xh(x)xh(x)xh(x) with midpoint-symmetric hhh Replace the weighted input by the midpoint after proving symmetry
Symmetric bounds [−a,a][-a,a][−a,a] Check the whole integrand for parity or complementary pairs
Modulus or floor Mark sign/step changes before integrating
Complete cycles Find the period of the actual integrand, including its modulus
Moving integration limits Fundamental theorem plus each bound's derivative
∑\sum∑ with large nnn Factor out the correct strip width and recognize the sample input
A positive product with an nnnth root Normalize, take logs, then recognize a rectangle sum
A high polynomial over a lower-degree polynomial Divide first
Infinite bound or log endpoint Establish the endpoint limit before using cancellation

Standard values worth recalling, with their reasons already taught:

∫01dx1+x2=π4,∫0π/2sin⁡x dx=∫0π/2cos⁡x dx=1,∫0π/2sin⁡2x dx=π4,∫0π/2sin⁡xcos⁡x dx=12,∫0π/2ln⁡(sin⁡x)dx=∫0π/2ln⁡(cos⁡x)dx=−π2ln⁡2,∫0πdxa+bcos⁡x=πa2−b2(a>∣b∣).\begin{gathered} \int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\frac\pi4,\qquad \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx=1,\\ \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2x\,dx=\frac\pi4,\qquad \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\cos x\,dx=\frac12,\\ \int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)dx =\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\cos x)dx=-\frac\pi2\ln2,\\ \int_0^\pi\frac{dx}{a+b\cos x} =\frac\pi{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}\qquad(a>|b|). \end{gathered}∫01​1+x2dx​=4π​,∫0π/2​sinxdx=∫0π/2​cosxdx=1,∫0π/2​sin2xdx=4π​,∫0π/2​sinxcosxdx=21​,∫0π/2​ln(sinx)dx=∫0π/2​ln(cosx)dx=−2π​ln2,∫0π​a+bcosxdx​=a2−b2​π​(a>∣b∣).​

The final row comes from t=tan⁡(x/2)t=\tan(x/2)t=tan(x/2): 2∫0∞dt/[(a+b)+(a−b)t2]2\int_0^\infty dt/[(a+b)+(a-b)t^2]2∫0∞​dt/[(a+b)+(a−b)t2]. Both coefficients are positive under a>∣b∣a>|b|a>∣b∣; changing that condition can introduce a singularity.

∫abf=F(b)−F(a),∫abf=∫abf(a+b−x)dx,f(x)+f(a+b−x)=K⇒∫abf=K(b−a)2,h(a+b−x)=h(x)⇒∫abxh(x)dx=a+b2∫abh(x)dx,∫−aaodd=0,∫−aaeven=2∫0aeven,ddx∫u(x)v(x)f(t)dt=f(v)v′−f(u)u′,1n∑r=1nf(r/n)→∫01f,Sn=n−1nSn−2, S0=π2, S1=1,∫0π∣sin⁡x∣dx=2,∫0nTf=n∫0Tf(T a period),∫ab∣f∣ is total area for a<b,x2=∣x∣.\begin{gathered} \int_a^bf=F(b)-F(a),\quad \int_a^bf=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)dx,\\ f(x)+f(a+b-x)=K\Rightarrow\int_a^bf=\frac{K(b-a)}2,\\ h(a+b-x)=h(x)\Rightarrow\int_a^b xh(x)dx=\frac{a+b}2\int_a^bh(x)dx,\\ \int_{-a}^a\text{odd}=0,\quad \int_{-a}^a\text{even}=2\int_0^a\text{even},\\ \frac d{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)dt=f(v)v'-f(u)u',\\ \frac1n\sum_{r=1}^nf(r/n)\to\int_0^1f,\quad S_n=\frac{n-1}nS_{n-2},\ S_0=\frac\pi2,\ S_1=1,\\ \int_0^\pi|\sin x|dx=2,\quad \int_0^{nT}f=n\int_0^Tf\quad(T\text{ a period}),\\ \int_a^b|f|\text{ is total area for }a<b,\qquad \sqrt{x^2}=|x|. \end{gathered}∫ab​f=F(b)−F(a),∫ab​f=∫ab​f(a+b−x)dx,f(x)+f(a+b−x)=K⇒∫ab​f=2K(b−a)​,h(a+b−x)=h(x)⇒∫ab​xh(x)dx=2a+b​∫ab​h(x)dx,∫−aa​odd=0,∫−aa​even=2∫0a​even,dxd​∫u(x)v(x)​f(t)dt=f(v)v′−f(u)u′,n1​r=1∑n​f(r/n)→∫01​f,Sn​=nn−1​Sn−2​, S0​=2π​, S1​=1,∫0π​∣sinx∣dx=2,∫0nT​f=n∫0T​f(T a period),∫ab​∣f∣ is total area for a<b,x2​=∣x∣.​

All integrals in property formulas must exist with the stated ordinary or convergent improper meaning. Before submitting: check the limits, signs, symmetry condition, modulus breakpoints and requested rounding.

Worked solutions to the 40 PDF questions

Read the question first. Notice the pattern, choose a route, then calculate. Alternative methods below are fully visible.

Question 1 — Reflection swaps sine and cosine

PDF page 64 | MCQ | Notes: C04

The value of ∫0π/2sin⁡3xsin⁡3x+cos⁡3x dx\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x}{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}\,dx∫0π/2​sin3x+cos3xsin3x​dx is

  • (a) π2\dfrac\pi22π​
  • (b) π8\dfrac\pi88π​
  • (c) π4\dfrac\pi44π​
  • (d) 3π4\dfrac{3\pi}443π​

Did you notice the same two cubes in the denominator? On [0,π/2][0,\pi/2][0,π/2], reflection x↦π/2−xx\mapsto\pi/2-xx↦π/2−x swaps sine and cosine.

Let the integral be III. Its reflected version is

I=∫0π/2cos⁡3xcos⁡3x+sin⁡3xdx.I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^3x}{\cos^3x+\sin^3x}dx.I=∫0π/2​cos3x+sin3xcos3x​dx.

Add:

2I=∫0π/21 dx=π2⇒I=π4(c).2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\frac\pi2 \Rightarrow\boxed{I=\frac\pi4}\quad\text{(c)}.2I=∫0π/2​1dx=2π​⇒I=4π​​(c).

The denominator is positive throughout this interval. A tangent substitution could produce a rational integral, but reflection gives the definite value immediately and avoids finding a primitive.

Question 2 — An even numerator works with a complementary denominator pair

PDF page 64 | MCQ | Notes: C06

∫−π/2π/2sin⁡2x1+ex dx\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2x}{1+e^x}\,dx∫−π/2π/2​1+exsin2x​dx equals

  • (a) π4\dfrac\pi44π​
  • (b) π2\dfrac\pi22π​
  • (c) π\piπ
  • (d) π8\dfrac\pi88π​

The whole function is not even, but its reflected partner is useful. The numerator stays sin⁡2x\sin^2xsin2x, while exe^xex becomes e−xe^{-x}e−x.

11+ex+11+e−x=1.\frac1{1+e^x}+\frac1{1+e^{-x}}=1.1+ex1​+1+e−x1​=1.

Thus

2I=∫−π/2π/2sin⁡2x dx=2∫0π/21−cos⁡2x2dx=π2.2I=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^2x\,dx =2\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1-\cos2x}2dx =\frac\pi2.2I=∫−π/2π/2​sin2xdx=2∫0π/2​21−cos2x​dx=2π​.

Therefore I=π/4\boxed{I=\pi/4}I=π/4​, (a). Do not apply the even-function rule to the original integrand; we proved a complementary-pair identity instead.

Question 3 — A symmetric weight replaces x by the midpoint

PDF page 64 | MCQ | Notes: C05

The value of ∫0πxsin⁡x1+cos⁡2x dx\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx∫0π​1+cos2xxsinx​dx is

  • (a) π22\dfrac{\pi^2}22π2​
  • (b) π28\dfrac{\pi^2}88π2​
  • (c) π4\dfrac\pi44π​
  • (d) π24\dfrac{\pi^2}44π2​

Separate the extra xxx from its weight. Put h(x)=sin⁡x/(1+cos⁡2x)h(x)=\sin x/(1+\cos^2x)h(x)=sinx/(1+cos2x). Because sin⁡(π−x)=sin⁡x\sin(\pi-x)=\sin xsin(π−x)=sinx and cos⁡2(π−x)=cos⁡2x\cos^2(\pi-x)=\cos^2xcos2(π−x)=cos2x, the weight is symmetric.

Reflection gives I=∫0π(π−x)h(x)dxI=\int_0^\pi(\pi-x)h(x)dxI=∫0π​(π−x)h(x)dx. Add it to the original:

2I=π∫0πh(x)dx.2I=\pi\int_0^\pi h(x)dx.2I=π∫0π​h(x)dx.

Now u=cos⁡xu=\cos xu=cosx, du=−sin⁡x dxdu=-\sin x\,dxdu=−sinxdx:

∫0πh(x)dx=∫−11du1+u2=π2.\int_0^\pi h(x)dx =\int_{-1}^1\frac{du}{1+u^2} =\frac\pi2.∫0π​h(x)dx=∫−11​1+u2du​=2π​.

Hence I=π2/4\boxed{I=\pi^2/4}I=π2/4​, (d).

Direct u=cos⁡xu=\cos xu=cosx in the original integral would turn xxx into cos⁡−1u\cos^{-1}ucos−1u, adding work. Remove the weighted input by symmetry first. Notice that option (c) lacks a square on π\piπ.

Question 4 — Split where the expression inside the modulus changes sign

PDF page 64 | MCQ | Notes: C08

The value of ∫02∣x2−x∣ dx\displaystyle\int_0^2|x^2-x|\,dx∫02​∣x2−x∣dx is

  • (a) 43\dfrac4334​
  • (b) 111
  • (c) 23\dfrac2332​
  • (d) 76\dfrac7667​

The modulus asks us to make the negative part positive. The inside is x(x−1)x(x-1)x(x−1): negative on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), positive on (1,2)(1,2)(1,2).

I=∫01(x−x2)dx+∫12(x2−x)dx=[x22−x33]01+[x33−x22]12=16+56=1(b).\begin{aligned} I&=\int_0^1(x-x^2)dx+\int_1^2(x^2-x)dx\\ &=\left[\frac{x^2}2-\frac{x^3}3\right]_0^1 +\left[\frac{x^3}3-\frac{x^2}2\right]_1^2\\ &=\frac16+\frac56=\boxed1\quad\text{(b)}. \end{aligned}I​=∫01​(x−x2)dx+∫12​(x2−x)dx=[2x2​−3x3​]01​+[3x3​−2x2​]12​=61​+65​=1​(b).​

Without the modulus, the answer would be 2/32/32/3. Integrating the polynomial first and putting a modulus around the final number does not give total area.

Question 5 — A convergent log singularity can be handled by symmetry

PDF page 64 | MCQ | Notes: C04,C13

∫0π/2ln⁡(sin⁡x) dx\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)\,dx∫0π/2​ln(sinx)dx equals

  • (a) π2ln⁡2\dfrac\pi2\ln22π​ln2
  • (b) −π2ln⁡2-\dfrac\pi2\ln2−2π​ln2
  • (c) −πln⁡2-\pi\ln2−πln2
  • (d) 000

First check the endpoint. Near 000, ln⁡(sin⁡x)=ln⁡x+ln⁡(sin⁡x/x)\ln(\sin x)=\ln x+\ln(\sin x/x)ln(sinx)=lnx+ln(sinx/x). The second part stays bounded, and ∫01∣ln⁡x∣dx\int_0^1|\ln x|dx∫01​∣lnx∣dx is finite. So this improper integral converges.

Let I=∫0π/2ln⁡(sin⁡x)dxI=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)dxI=∫0π/2​ln(sinx)dx. Reflection gives the same III for ln⁡(cos⁡x)\ln(\cos x)ln(cosx). Add:

2I=∫0π/2ln⁡(sin⁡xcos⁡x)dx=∫0π/2ln⁡(sin⁡2x)dx−π2ln⁡2.2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x\cos x)dx =\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin2x)dx-\frac\pi2\ln2.2I=∫0π/2​ln(sinxcosx)dx=∫0π/2​ln(sin2x)dx−2π​ln2.

For the remaining integral, put u=2xu=2xu=2x. Symmetry of sin⁡u\sin usinu about π/2\pi/2π/2 gives

∫0π/2ln⁡(sin⁡2x)dx=12∫0πln⁡(sin⁡u)du=I.\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin2x)dx =\frac12\int_0^\pi\ln(\sin u)du=I.∫0π/2​ln(sin2x)dx=21​∫0π​ln(sinu)du=I.

Hence 2I=I−(π/2)ln⁡22I=I-(\pi/2)\ln22I=I−(π/2)ln2, so I=−(π/2)ln⁡2\boxed{I=-(\pi/2)\ln2}I=−(π/2)ln2​, (b). The negative answer matches the graph because 0<sin⁡x≤10<\sin x\le10<sinx≤1.

Question 6 — Reflection turns a logarithmic product into a constant

PDF page 64 | MCQ | Notes: C04

The value of ∫0π/4ln⁡(1+tan⁡x) dx\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan x)\,dx∫0π/4​ln(1+tanx)dx is

  • (a) π4ln⁡2\dfrac\pi4\ln24π​ln2
  • (b) π2ln⁡2\dfrac\pi2\ln22π​ln2
  • (c) π16ln⁡2\dfrac\pi{16}\ln216π​ln2
  • (d) π8ln⁡2\dfrac\pi8\ln28π​ln2

The upper bound π/4\pi/4π/4 suggests reflecting by π/4−x\pi/4-xπ/4−x. Let t=tan⁡xt=\tan xt=tanx. The reflected tangent is (1−t)/(1+t)(1-t)/(1+t)(1−t)/(1+t).

(1+t)(1+1−t1+t)=2.(1+t)\left(1+\frac{1-t}{1+t}\right)=2.(1+t)(1+1+t1−t​)=2.

So the two reflected logarithms add to ln⁡2\ln2ln2.

2I=∫0π/4ln⁡2 dx=π4ln⁡2⇒I=π8ln⁡2(d).2I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln2\,dx=\frac\pi4\ln2 \Rightarrow\boxed{I=\frac\pi8\ln2}\quad\text{(d)}.2I=∫0π/4​ln2dx=4π​ln2⇒I=8π​ln2​(d).

Both log inputs are positive and finite. Expanding ln⁡(1+tan⁡x)\ln(1+\tan x)ln(1+tanx) into a series is possible only with extra convergence care and is much longer than this exact pair.

Question 7 — Count complete periods after applying the modulus

PDF page 64 | Numerical value | Notes: C07

The value of ∫025π∣sin⁡x∣ dx\displaystyle\int_0^{25\pi}|\sin x|\,dx∫025π​∣sinx∣dx is ____.

The modulus changes the period. Every negative sine hump is flipped upwards, so ∣sin⁡x∣|\sin x|∣sinx∣ repeats after π\piπ.

One hump contributes

∫0π∣sin⁡x∣dx=∫0πsin⁡x dx=[−cos⁡x]0π=2.\int_0^\pi|\sin x|dx=\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx =[-\cos x]_0^\pi=2.∫0π​∣sinx∣dx=∫0π​sinxdx=[−cosx]0π​=2.

There are 252525 complete periods, so I=25(2)=50I=25(2)=\boxed{50}I=25(2)=50​. Using the ordinary sine's full-cycle cancellation would ignore the modulus.

Question 8 — The interval endpoints tell us the reflection sum

PDF page 64 | MCQ | Notes: C04

∫π/6π/3dx1+tan⁡x\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\frac{dx}{1+\sqrt{\tan x}}∫π/6π/3​1+tanx​dx​ equals

  • (a) π12\dfrac\pi{12}12π​
  • (b) π6\dfrac\pi66π​
  • (c) π3\dfrac\pi33π​
  • (d) π24\dfrac\pi{24}24π​

Use the endpoint sum, not only the upper endpoint. Here π/6+π/3=π/2\pi/6+\pi/3=\pi/2π/6+π/3=π/2, so reflection is x↦π/2−xx\mapsto\pi/2-xx↦π/2−x.

Since tan⁡(π/2−x)=1/tan⁡x\tan(\pi/2-x)=1/\tan xtan(π/2−x)=1/tanx and tangent is positive here, put u=tan⁡x>0u=\sqrt{\tan x}>0u=tanx​>0:

11+u+11+1/u=1.\frac1{1+u}+\frac1{1+1/u}=1.1+u1​+1+1/u1​=1.

Therefore 2I=π/3−π/6=π/62I=\pi/3-\pi/6=\pi/62I=π/3−π/6=π/6 and I=π/12\boxed{I=\pi/12}I=π/12​, (a). The square root causes no sign ambiguity because tangent is positive throughout the interval.

Question 9 — A simple substitution avoids a ten-term expansion

PDF page 65 | MCQ | Notes: C03,C09

The value of ∫01x(1−x)10 dx\displaystyle\int_0^1x(1-x)^{10}\,dx∫01​x(1−x)10dx is

  • (a) 1110\dfrac1{110}1101​
  • (b) 1121\dfrac1{121}1211​
  • (c) 1132\dfrac1{132}1321​
  • (d) 166\dfrac1{66}661​

Expanding (1−x)10(1-x)^{10}(1−x)10 would create eleven terms. Instead let the repeated bracket itself be u=1−xu=1-xu=1−x. Then x=1−ux=1-ux=1−u, dx=−dudx=-dudx=−du, and bounds 0,10,10,1 become 1,01,01,0:

I=∫10(1−u)u10(−du)=∫01(u10−u11)du=111−112=1132(c).I=\int_1^0(1-u)u^{10}(-du) =\int_0^1(u^{10}-u^{11})du =\frac1{11}-\frac1{12} =\boxed{\frac1{132}}\quad\text{(c)}.I=∫10​(1−u)u10(−du)=∫01​(u10−u11)du=111​−121​=1321​​(c).

Another possible approach: the finite factorial result from C09 gives 1! 10!/12!=1/(12⋅11)1!\,10!/12!=1/(12\cdot11)1!10!/12!=1/(12⋅11). The one-substitution route is shorter and shows why a large exponent need not mean a long calculation.

Question 10 — Reduce an even sine power two steps at a time
